topic: Make Claude's writing sound plain and human instead of generic: a standing style instruction, plain-language rules from official government and industry sources, a swap list of words and patterns, and a research-first prompt to run before any writing
audience: Professionals who use Claude to draft emails, reports, posts and instructions, and find the drafts polished but bland, wordy and obviously generic
goal: Save one short plain-English style instruction in Claude, use a swap list and a research-first prompt, and run a plain-language check on every draft before it goes out
notes: Anthropic's prompting guide says to treat Claude like a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows: the more precisely you explain what you want, the better the result. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices]

Anthropic's key test for a prompt: show it to a colleague with minimal context on the task; if they would be confused, Claude will be too. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices]

Be specific about the output format and constraints, and if you want more than the minimum, ask for it explicitly. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices]

Give the reason behind an instruction: Anthropic's example replaces 'NEVER use ellipses' with the explanation that the reply will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine, because Claude can generalize from the explanation. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices]

Anthropic calls examples one of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure. Its article for Claude app users (10 Nov 2025) advises starting with one example and adding more only if the output still doesn't match, and notes that Claude 4.x and similar models pay very close attention to details in examples. [https://claude.com/resources/articles/best-practices-for-prompt-engineering]

To control formatting, tell Claude what to do rather than what not to do (ask for 'smoothly flowing prose paragraphs' instead of 'Do not use markdown'), and match your prompt's own style to the output you want. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices]

Setting a role focuses Claude's behavior and tone; Anthropic says even a single sentence makes a difference. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices]

Anthropic's claude.com article warns against over-engineering: longer, more complex prompts are not always better, the first prompt rarely works perfectly, and you should test and refine. [https://claude.com/resources/articles/best-practices-for-prompt-engineering]

To reduce hallucinations, explicitly give Claude permission to say 'I don't know'; Anthropic says this can drastically reduce false information. For long documents, ask Claude to extract word-for-word quotes first and base its answer on them, and to back each claim with a supporting quote or retract it; these reduce but do not eliminate hallucinations. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations]

Claude can hallucinate incorrect or misleading information; Anthropic says not to rely on it as a singular source of truth and to scrutinize high-stakes advice and check cited sources. [https://support.claude.com/en/articles/8525154-claude-is-providing-incorrect-or-misleading-responses-what-s-going-on]

Web search is turned on in a chat with '+' > 'Web search' and returns answers with citations; in the new Claude experience there is no toggle and Claude searches when it helps. Free accounts can use it. [https://support.claude.com/en/articles/10684626-enable-and-use-web-search]

Research (paid plans) runs multiple searches that build on each other across the web and connected tools; it needs web search on and is turned on with '+' > 'Research'. [https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11088861-use-research-on-claude]

Account-wide Instructions are set in Settings > Your Claude > Instructions and apply to all conversations; project instructions apply within a project; skills customize how Claude formats and delivers responses. [https://support.claude.com/en/articles/10185728-understanding-claude-s-personalization-features]

To create a project, go to claude.ai/projects and click '+ New Project'; add files with '+' and instructions with 'Set project instructions'. The projects help page says projects are available to all users and Free users can create up to five, but the personalization page says project instructions are for paid plans only. [https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9519177-how-can-i-create-and-manage-projects]

The US Plain Writing Act of 2010 (Public Law 111-274) defines plain writing as writing that is clear, concise, well-organized and suited to the subject and audience. [https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-111publ274/html/PLAW-111publ274.htm]

PlainLanguage.gov now redirects to digital.gov/guides/plain-language, where the US General Services Administration's Digital.gov carries forward selected PlainLanguage.gov content. [https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language]

Digital.gov's first rule of plain language is to write for your audience; it calls 'dumbing down' a common myth and says to match your readers' knowledge, expertise and interest. [https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language/principles]

Digital.gov: express only one idea in each sentence; writing experts recommend paragraphs of no more than 150 words in three to eight sentences, and never longer than 250 words. [https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language/writing/clear-short]

Digital.gov: cut filler modifiers such as absolutely, actually, completely, really, quite, totally and very, which are usually unnecessary and may even be nonsensical. [https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language/principles/short-simple]

Digital.gov says readers complain about jargon more than any other writing fault: use everyday language where you can, and define a necessary technical term where you use it. [https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language/principles/avoid-jargon]

Plain English is mandatory for all of GOV.UK; the Government Digital Service cites literacy data such as 1 in 6 adults in England having very poor literacy skills. [https://guidance.publishing.service.gov.uk/writing-to-gov-uk-standards/writing-guidelines/clear-language/]

GOV.UK: do not use formal or long words when short ones will do: 'buy' not 'purchase', 'help' not 'assist', 'about' not 'approximately'. [https://guidance.publishing.service.gov.uk/writing-to-gov-uk-standards/writing-guidelines/clear-language/]

GOV.UK: paragraphs should have no more than 5 sentences each, and try to split up sentences over 25 words long. [https://guidance.publishing.service.gov.uk/writing-to-gov-uk-standards/writing-guidelines/clear-language/]

GOV.UK prefers the active voice because it is more direct and keeps sentences short: 'You need an electronic travel authorisation', not 'An electronic travel authorisation is needed'. [https://guidance.publishing.service.gov.uk/writing-to-gov-uk-standards/writing-guidelines/clear-language/]

GOV.UK: write conversationally, as if talking to the reader one-to-one but with the authority of someone who can actively help, and address the user as 'you' where possible. [https://guidance.publishing.service.gov.uk/writing-to-gov-uk-standards/writing-guidelines/right-tone/]

GOV.UK: frontload content by putting the most important information first; GDS says most people read only 20 to 28% of the text on a webpage. [https://guidance.publishing.service.gov.uk/writing-to-gov-uk-standards/writing-guidelines/clear-structure/]

The GOV.UK A to Z style guide keeps a 'Words to avoid' list: 'utilise' becomes 'use', 'collaborate' becomes 'work with', 'leverage' becomes 'influence' or 'use'. [https://guidance.publishing.service.gov.uk/writing-to-gov-uk-standards/style-guides/a-to-z-style-guide/]

ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (STE) is a controlled language first released in 1986 to help readers of English maintenance documentation. It has 53 writing rules and a dictionary of about 900 approved words, each with one meaning. [https://www.asd-ste100.org/about_STE.html]
STE caps procedural sentences (instructions) at 20 words and descriptive sentences at 25 words (Issue 9, Rules 5.1 and 6.3). [https://zenodo.org/records/23666006]

STE writes procedures in the imperative (command) form, for example 'Install the component.'; it is not meant for general-purpose writing, but ASD says its principles, like short sentences, one topic per sentence and the active voice, work well in other writing. [https://www.asd-ste100.org/STE_faq.html]

ASD's STE working group white paper on STE and AI (June 2026) says AI tools can support writing but cannot replace human oversight: AI should assist, not replace, human authors. [https://www.asd-ste100.org/assets/files/WhitePaper-ASD-STE100_and_AI.pdf]
Mojeed Abisiga is a data and AI leader and educator whose mission is to make data and AI easy for everyone; he teaches people to use AI at work. [https://mojeedabisiga.com/]
